strengths: Novel meta-AFA problem formulation addressing retrospective missingness with sound theoretical foundations (Theorems 3.4, 4.2)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (GP, MiniBooNE, MNIST, Metabric, MIMIC-IV) with systematic study of varying context lengths and missingness rates
Improved uncertainty quantification demonstrated consistently (Figures 3, 7) with better calibration than task-specific baselines, particularly as features accumulate
Elegant in-context learning approach eliminating per-task retraining, offering practical computational savings
Honest and rigorous experimental reporting with good acknowledgment of limitations and ablation studies showing when adaptivity helps/hurts
Strong reproducibility with comprehensive hyperparameters, detailed experimental setup, promised code release, and adequate documentation
weaknesses: Limited real-world empirical gains: Performance on real datasets (MIMIC, Metabric) shows marginal improvements or performance indistinguishable from baselines (Figures 8-9); adaptivity sometimes provides no benefit (Fig 13)

Restrictive and unverifiable assumptions: MAR is untestable; blocked policies prevent generalization to tasks with different missingness patterns; positivity/sufficient coverage is vague with no practical verification methods or robustness analysis

Scalability limitations: Only evaluated on small feature sets (≤20 features); no high-dimensional experiments; computational cost of L2M vs baselines not compared; DQN excluded from synthetic tasks due to computational constraints

Semi-synthetic evaluation introduces distribution shift: BNN priors for training + real labels for testing limits confidence in transfer; paper acknowledges performance 'depends on alignment' but doesn't systematically characterize when transfer succeeds/fails

Technical gaps: Gumbel-Softmax bias impact not quantified; surrogate loss optimality relies on Covert et al.'s practical heuristic rather than principled approximation; sequence model approximates Bayesian inference via inductive biases—a still-debated connection

Missing critical analyses: No failure mode investigation; no ablations on architecture choices; no investigation of learned patterns; no computational time comparisons; blocked policy constraint not discussed as potential limitation for generalization

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing meta-AFA with retrospective missingness using principled causal framework (Theorem 3.4 on CMI identification under MAR is rigorous)
Strong uncertainty quantification results: Figure 3 convincingly demonstrates L2M provides better calibrated uncertainty than task-specific baselines, especially as more features are acquired
Comprehensive experimental scope spanning synthetic (GP/Matern), semi-synthetic (BNN priors with real features), and real datasets (MIMIC, Metabric, MNIST)
Practical contribution via blocked policies that avoid full generative modeling while handling unobserved features
Extensive appendix with algorithmic details, proofs, and hyperparameter specifications supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Theory-practice gap: Theorem 4.2 guarantees *any minimizer* recovers CMI-optimal actions, but no analysis of whether gradient-based optimization achieves such a minimizer, how far it deviates, or how Gumbel-softmax bias affects guarantees. Connection between sequence modeling and posterior recovery under missingness is informal.

Mixed and modest empirical results on real data (primary concern for significance): Metabric shows marginal gains, MiniBooNE/MIMIC tasks have inconsistent benefits, and paper admits 'adaptive strategies offer only marginal gains over random acquisition on some real datasets.' Strong results only on synthetic data closest to pretraining prior.

Restrictive, untestable assumptions: MAR assumption frequently violated in clinical data; positivity requires sufficient feature coverage (unverified); exclusion restriction questionable in settings where measurement affects decisions. Conditional independence across queries (Assumption A.5) buried in appendix.

Pretraining-task-alignment dependency undermines generality: Figure 8 shows performance on real tasks is 'mixed and dependent on whether pretraining BNN tasks are closely aligned.' Paper defers principled prior specification to future work, suggesting core practical limitation.

Limited technical novelty: Theorem 3.4 is standard causal identification (Rubin 1976); Theorem 4.2 is incremental extension of Covert et al. (2023); sequence models for meta-learning are established. Main contribution is straightforward combination of existing techniques.

Unfair baseline comparisons: Task-specific baselines (GDFS, DIME) trained only on individual test tasks lack access to meta-pretraining data, creating artificial disadvantage. DQN excluded from synthetic experiments due to computational cost. No comparison to task-specific models with access to pretraining pool.

Insufficient ablation studies: Custom attention masking, removal of positional embeddings, and architectural choices justified only by reference to invariance properties (Definitions A.6-A.7) without empirical validation. No ablations on sequence length sensitivity, pretraining prior sensitivity, or value of blocked policies.

Missing investigation of when adaptivity matters: Figure 12 shows simpler tasks (MiniBooNE) show no benefit from adaptive selection; Figure 13 shows some real tasks (Readmission) don't benefit from adaptivity. Raises question: when is adaptive AFA necessary in practice?

Semi-synthetic evaluation limits real-world assessment: Pretraining uses synthetic BNN labels, testing uses real labels. Obscures whether gains come from accurate uncertainty quantification or learning real label distribution. No validation that learned policies match clinical guidelines or improve real outcomes.

Presentation issues: Heavy notation and key architectural details (Appendix A.4) make main text harder to follow; limited intuition for why sequence models specifically address missingness beyond flexibility; no ablation on proposed architectural modifications

strengths: Novel meta-AFA problem formulation addressing practical challenge of retrospective missingness with real healthcare motivation
Solid theoretical contributions: Theorem 3.4 establishes identifiability of CMI under MAR/exclusion restriction/positivity; Theorem 4.2 rigorously connects surrogate loss to CMI-optimal acquisition
Principled technical approach using sequence modeling for uncertainty quantification, blocked policies to avoid full generative modeling, and differentiable optimization via Gumbel-softmax

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: multiple data sources (synthetic GP, semi-synthetic BNN, real datasets), systematic UQ evaluation, honest reporting of context-dependent performance, thoughtful ablations
Targeted improvements in scarce-label, high-missingness regimes where need is greatest (Figure 5); reliable uncertainty coverage (Figure 3)
Strong reproducibility practices: detailed hyperparameters, dataset specifications, algorithms, code release promised
Clear, well-motivated presentation with effective use of examples and principled framework design
weaknesses: Exclusion restriction assumption (3.2) is restrictive and potentially violated in healthcare motivating example: measuring a feature can trigger interventions that affect outcome
Strong identifying assumptions (MAR, exclusion restriction, positivity) are untestable; paper provides no practical diagnostics for violations or guidance on when assumptions fail

Theory-practice gap: Theorem 3.4 requires pointwise identification for all states, but authors acknowledge this unnecessary in practice; blocked policy constraint deviates from theoretical optimum with no formal performance degradation analysis
Mixed empirical results on real data: Figures 8 and 13 show inconsistent improvements on real tasks; performance heavily dependent on task prior alignment, limiting practical applicability

Dependence on task prior specification: paper provides limited guidance for practitioners on how to choose appropriate prior or assess robustness to misspecification; BNN prior may not match real test distribution
Incomplete ablations: no ablation on blocked policy impact, no comparison of surrogate loss vs. true CMI, no analysis of Gumbel-softmax bias effects

Semi-synthetic experimental design: using BNN priors during training but real labels at test creates domain gap that may not reflect true distribution shift; limits conclusions about real-world performance
Limited scope: time-invariant setting excludes temporal dynamics, uniform feature costs unrealistic, no analysis of scaling to high-dimensional problems or complex domains
Uncertainty quantification gains on in-distribution tasks (Figure 3) but more mixed on real data (Figure 8); connection between improved UQ and AFA performance not always evident
Missing important comparisons: no evaluation against methods using unlabeled data, no analysis of performance scaling with budget k, limited discussion of failure modes

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation with explicit treatment of retrospective missingness, addressing a practically important limitation of existing AFA methods
Solid theoretical contributions including identifiability of CMI under missingness (Theorem 3.4) and optimality guarantees for sequence loss objective (Theorem 4.2)
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple domains (synthetic, semi-synthetic, real) with multiple evaluation metrics showing robustness to limited labeled data and high missingness rates
Avoids expensive posterior sampling through sequence modeling, providing practical scalability advantages over prior generative modeling approaches
Honest and thorough discussion of limitations with extensive ablations and stress tests in appendix
weaknesses: Significant gap between theory and practice: Theorem 4.2 assumes perfect optimization, but implementation uses biased gradient estimator (straight-through Gumbel-softmax); Figure 17 shows non-negligible bias but impact on theoretical guarantees not characterized

Greedy policies fundamentally limited for jointly informative features (acknowledged in Appendix A.4 but deserves more prominence); lookahead variant shows only modest improvements (Figure 5) while increasing computational cost

Strong, unverifiable assumptions (MAR, Positivity, No Direct Effect) with no practical diagnostics for violations; Positivity especially problematic—requires sufficient data coverage of each feature action, easily violated in practice

Limited practical improvements on real data: Figure 8 shows mixed results with overlapping confidence intervals; MIMIC improvements are modest (~0.02 NLL); Figure 14 shows fully synthetic pretraining requires task-specific fine-tuning, undermining efficiency claims

Proof-of-concept status limits impact: Authors acknowledge lack of deployment readiness, scalability undemonstrated, semi-synthetic evaluation may not reflect realistic scenarios, and no evidence of clinical utility/interpretability important for healthcare deployment

Methodological concerns: baseline modifications (fixed vs. decay schedules) may not represent methods at their best; DQN excluded from synthetic tasks; potential domain shift from semi-synthetic pretraining to real test labels

Technical contributions are incremental: combines existing techniques (sequence models for uncertainty, CMI selection, Gumbel-softmax) rather than novel algorithms; builds directly on recent sequence-modeling-for-Bayesian-inference work

strengths: Principled treatment of retrospective missingness with clear identification conditions (Theorem 3.4) under MAR, no direct effect, and positivity assumptions
Well-executed end-to-end technical framework combining sequence modeling, uncertainty quantification, and differentiable policy optimization with proper theoretical grounding (Theorem 4.2)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning synthetic (GP, BNN), semi-synthetic (MIMIC, Metabric), and real-world (MNIST) datasets with multiple metrics (log loss, MSE, AUROC, coverage)
Solid practical implementation details with complete algorithms, hyperparameters, and reproducibility documentation in appendix
Honest discussion of limitations and careful positioning as proof-of-concept work requiring prospective validation
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (transformers for sequence modeling, greedy CMI from Covert et al. 2023, standard meta-learning) without significant new methodological insights

Strong, partly untestable theoretical assumptions: MAR is untestable; no-direct-effect assumption is violated in medical settings where measurements affect clinical decisions; positivity and conditional independence lack validation or sensitivity analysis

Weak real-world validation: most clear improvements are on synthetic/semi-synthetic tasks; Figure 14 shows poor generalization from purely synthetic pretraining; improvements on actual real-world tasks are modest and within confidence intervals

Unresolved task prior specification problem: acknowledged limitation but no principled procedure provided; practitioners unclear how to specify priors for new domains; strong dependence on prior specification contradicts generalization claims
Blocked policies constraint is overly conservative: restricts to features seen in training data, contradicting MAR assumption; policy cannot strategically attempt acquiring unseen features

Missing critical baseline comparisons: no comparison with recent meta-learning approaches, tabular foundation models (TabPFN), or other recent methods; DQN excluded from synthetic experiments due to 'computational cost'
Two-stage training (predictor then policy) lacks ablation study; no investigation of joint training; Gumbel-softmax bias not thoroughly analyzed despite being fundamental to gradient estimation

No statistical significance testing in main results (Figure 4); marginal improvements on Metabric; confidence intervals overlap on real-world tasks; unclear when L2M outperforms task-specific fine-tuning

Theoretical contributions are incremental: Theorem 3.4 applies standard causal identification results; Theorem 4.2 is sketched in main text with full proof in appendix; gap between surrogate loss and true CMI not characterized

Uncertainty quantification claims overstated: Figure 3 shows only incremental improvements in calibration over MLP; advantage diminishes as more features acquired; evaluated only on in-distribution synthetic tasks

strengths: Well-motivated problem with practical relevance: addresses sequential feature acquisition under retrospective missingness, important for cost-sensitive applications like clinical diagnostics
Solid theoretical contributions: Theorem 3.4 formally establishes CMI identifiability under realistic causal assumptions; Theorem 4.2 connects sequence loss to CMI-optimal acquisition
Principled approach: elegant integration of sequence modeling for uncertainty with differentiable policy learning; blocked policy design sensibly handles training constraints

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: multiple synthetic priors, real-world datasets, thorough ablations, beyond-accuracy metrics (coverage, calibration, log loss), length generalization demonstrated
Consistent improvements in targeted regime: L2M shows notable gains under scarce labels and high missingness (Figure 11), aligning with motivation
Clear presentation: generally well-written with good problem formulation and informative figures; explicit treatment of retrospective missingness is valuable
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: sequence modeling for Bayesian inference, CMI objectives, and Gumbel-Softmax are existing techniques; contribution is primarily in combination

Heavy dependence on task prior quality: Figure 14 shows substantial degradation with task mismatch; no principled method for constructing priors; Figure 8 reveals mixed real-world performance; lacks guidance on when L2M should be preferred

Theoretical gaps: Theorem 4.2 proof sketched with restrictive assumptions; applies only to cross-entropy loss; no finite-sample complexity analysis; approximation error of one-step surrogate (Eq. 5) not quantified

Evaluation methodology concerns: most strong results on semi-synthetic tasks from same BNN prior as training (within-prior generalization); real-world out-of-distribution performance mixed (Appendix Figures 8, 14, 16); DQN excluded from synthetic tasks limiting baseline comparisons

Limited robustness analysis: MAR/positivity/no-direct-effect assumptions untestable; no diagnostic methods for violations; time-invariant assumption restrictive; minimal empirical sensitivity analysis

Scalability and practical concerns: requires 4 H100 GPUs and 10 hours pretraining per prior; no analysis with high-dimensional features; blocked policy requires knowing feature availability; limited deployment guidance for new domains
Lookahead results underwhelming: 1-step lookahead provides marginal gains (Figure 5); planning variant insufficiently evaluated in main text despite being claimed contribution

Experimental fairness: task-specific baselines train on single task while L2M leverages diverse prior—not entirely comparable; mixed results on truly unseen real tasks without task-specific fine-tuning (Figure 14)
